outcomes: Finds the capture that takes away the only defender of a piece
Counts the defenders of the target before capturing one
Says why a second defender or a cheaper recapture defeats the idea
sources: sources/sheets/edlasker_chess-strategy.md (K3: three ways the count lies)
sources/sheets/nimzowitsch_my-system.md (idea 27: exchange on the pinning square)

steps.text: A defended piece is only safe while its defender stays. If one piece does all the defending, **capture that defender** and the target is left without protection. This is *removing the defender*. It is a capture, so it is the plainest of the ways to attack a defence. Look for the defender first, then ask what captures it.

Taking the defender is a trade, and a trade can go wrong. Before you capture, count: **who else defends the target?** And **what can recapture on the square you capture on?** The idea works only if the target ends up with no defender after the exchange.

steps.title: A second defender
steps.prompt: A white pawn on f2 now guards g3 as well.

steps.text: **When it holds:** the target has one defender and you can capture it; after the trades the target is still unprotected. **When it fails:** a second piece defends the target, or the defender is guarded so that your capture loses more than it wins. As a rule of thumb, count both before you take.

steps.prompt: When a piece looked defended, did you count every defender before you captured one?

steps.text: **Remember.** Removing the defender means capturing the one piece that protects a target, so the target is left unprotected. Before you capture, count who else defends the target and what can recapture. It fails when a second piece guards the target, or when your capture loses more than it wins.
